Subject: Scheduling approach for a multi‑mode, resource‑ and budget‑constrained project

Overview
We are preparing the baseline schedule for a project comprising multiple interdependent activities that draw on shared, limited resources. Each activity can be executed in one of several modes, reflecting different speed/cost/resource profiles. The scheduling challenge is to select one mode per activity and sequence the work so that all technical dependencies, timing windows, resource limits, and the overall budget are respected—while completing the project as quickly as possible.

Execution modes and non‑preemption
- Each activity offers alternative execution modes. Faster options typically shorten duration but consume more resources and cost more; slower options reduce spend and resource demand at the expense of time.
- Once an activity starts, it runs to completion without interruption. There is no splitting or pause/restart within an activity.

Dependencies and lags
- Activities have finish‑to‑start dependencies that must be honored.
- Some dependencies specify a minimum wait after a predecessor finishes (the successor cannot start before this minimum delay elapses).
- Some dependencies also impose a maximum wait (the successor must start within a specified time window after the predecessor finishes).
- These relationships create knock‑on effects: tighter maximum delays limit how much we can postpone successors, and longer minimum delays can push out downstream work.

Timing windows
- Selected activities have earliest allowed start times (release dates). These gates prevent work from beginning before certain dates or external prerequisites are met.
- Some activities carry hard deadlines that must be met; failure to finish by these dates is not acceptable.

Renewable resources and the conservative safety rule
- The project uses multiple renewable resource types with fixed, time‑based capacities. When an activity finishes, the resources it used return to the pool and can be reassigned.
- To prevent overloads in a simple, auditable way, we will apply a conservative safety rule for activities that are not directly linked by precedence: if there exists even one combination of their execution modes and at least one resource where their combined usage would exceed that resource’s capacity, those two activities cannot run at the same time and must be sequenced (one finishes before the other starts). This is the ONLY resource constraint — there is no separate "at all times" capacity check beyond these pairwise sequencing decisions.
- This rule intentionally errs on the side of caution: even if some mode pairings would fit, the potential for an overload in any pairing is enough to prohibit overlap. As a result, more resource‑hungry or faster modes can trigger additional sequencing requirements.

Budget constraint
- The total spend on selected execution modes is capped by a fixed project budget. The sum of the costs of the chosen modes across all activities must not exceed this limit.
- Faster modes may help meet tight lags or deadlines but will consume more of the budget; slower modes conserve spend but can extend the schedule and increase exposure to timing constraints.

Scheduling goal and trade‑offs
- Our goal is to finalize a feasible schedule that minimizes total project duration (makespan) while staying within budget and complying with all dependencies, lags, release dates, deadlines, and the safety‑based resource limits.
- Key trade‑offs include:
  - Speed vs. cost: selecting faster modes to compress the timeline versus slower modes to preserve budget.
  - Overlap vs. sequencing: choosing modes that avoid creating new sequencing conflicts under the safety rule versus modes that force more serial work.
  - Timing feasibility: aligning mode choices and task order with minimum/maximum lags, release dates, and deadlines.

Next steps
- Assemble the shortlist of viable mode selections per activity considering budget impact and potential safety‑rule conflicts.
- Identify and lock down the forced sequences implied by precedence and the safety rule.
- Build and review candidate schedules that meet all constraints, compare their completion dates and budget usage, and select the plan with the shortest duration that stays within the budget and timing commitments.
